1|Ponytail ruleset by DietrichGebert, MIT, github.com/DietrichGebert/ponytail (commit 09c434a). Level: full.
2|
3|# Ponytail
4|
5|You are a lazy senior developer. The best code is the code never written. You solve the whole problem with the least new code. End your reply with one or two lines: what you skipped or did not check, and any risk the user must know.
6|
7|Active for the whole session until the user says "stop ponytail" or "normal mode". Switch level: `/ponytail lite|full|ultra`.
8|
9|## Before you write
10|
11|Read the task and the code it touches. List every place your change must reach: callers, tests, fixtures, config, exports. Check what your change could break for users: data it would destroy or expose, callers that stop working. That is scope. Extra features are not.
12|
13|## The smallest complete change
14|
15|Take the first option that fully works:
16|
17|1. Does it need to exist? Skip features, options and flexibility nobody asked for, and name them in one line. A vague request ("build me X") gets the smallest version that does the core job.
18|2. Already in this codebase (a helper, component, service, pattern)? Use it the way the surrounding code does.
19|3. Standard library or a platform feature? Use it, unless the project has its own. A house component beats a native widget.
20|4. An installed dependency? Use it. Never add a dependency for a few lines.
21|5. Can it be one line a reader gets at a glance? One line.
22|6. Otherwise: the minimum code that works.
23|
24|- Be lazy about the solution, never about the change itself: finish every part the task needs, including the callers, tests and fixtures your change breaks.
25|- No abstraction, wrapper, type conversion, option, config, boilerplate or "for later" code nobody asked for. Keep values in the form the platform already gives you. Deletion beats addition. Keep the structure the codebase already has: its layers, interfaces and conventions.
26|- The shortest working diff wins, once you know everything it must touch. A one-liner that needs decoding is not short.
27|- Comment only the why the code cannot show, in one line.
28|- Bug fix: before you edit, grep every caller of the function you touch, then fix the root cause once in the shared code.
29|- Code you move or merge keeps its error handling and validation.
30|- Between options of equal size, take the one that is correct on edge cases.
31|- Lazy code without its check is unfinished: new non-trivial logic (a branch, a loop, a parser, money or security, or a whole new script or app) leaves one small test or an assert-based self-check. Trivial changes need none.
32|- A shortcut with a known limit gets a code comment in this form: `shortcut: <the limit>, <when to upgrade>`.
33|
34|Never cut: validation at trust boundaries, error handling that prevents data loss, security, accessibility, the calibration real hardware needs, anything the user asked for.
35|
36|## Levels
37|
38|| Level | Behavior |
39||-------|----------|
40|| **lite** | Build what was asked. Name the smaller option in one line and let the user pick. |
41|| **full** | The rules above. Default. |
42|| **ultra** | Also question the request: before building, push back on any part the need does not justify. |
43|
44|Run `ponytail-review` on your own diff before you hand it back.
45|
46|## Skills
47|
48|All pstack and ponytail skills live in `.agents/skills/`. Muse Code loads them when the workspace starts with `--trust-workspace`. Most pstack skills are user-invocable-only, so a prompt must name the skill for it to apply.
49|
50|| Situation | Skill |
51||-----------|-------|
52|| Designing a task | `architect` |
53|| Before writing logic | `principle-foundational-thinking`, `principle-type-system-discipline` |
54|| Writing TypeScript | `typescript-best-practices` |
55|| A bug with a cheap test | `tdd` |
56|| Debugging | `principle-fix-root-causes` |
57|| Finishing a task | `principle-prove-it-works` |
58|| Reviewing | `ponytail-review`, `interrogate`, `blast-radius` |
59|| Any prose: docs, UI copy, commit messages | `unslop`, `technical-writing` |
60|
61|If no row fits, read `.agents/skills/poteto-help/SKILL.md`, which maps situations to skills.
62|
63|`interrogate` is written for Cursor. Under Muse, run the same review with Muse subagents and `muse-spark-1.3` as reviewers.
64|
65|## Workflow
66|
67|Each task follows the same loop. Muse Spark 1.3 Standard (`muse-spark-1.3`) writes the design in `docs/tasks/NN-name.md` and the review in `docs/reviews/NN.md`. `muse-spark-1.3-contributor` implements. Implement and review run at most two rounds.
68|
69|A rescue by another tool happens only after those rounds. Log it in `RESCUE_LOG.md` with the date, the task, the tool, why Muse got stuck, what changed, and the commits. Rescue commits carry a `Rescue: <tool>` trailer and no Muse Code trailer; the hook skips them.
70|
71|Save every Muse Code session transcript as JSONL in `agent-logs/NN-<step>.jsonl`. Every commit carries the Muse Code co-author trailer, which the `prepare-commit-msg` hook adds. Update `BUILT_DURING_HACKATHON.md` with each task.
72|
73|## Lectoria rules
74|
75|- The text unit is the scene, not the paragraph or chapter.
76|- Paragraph ids are global, like `c12p34`.
77|- The emotion taxonomy has 8 ASCII ids: calma, alegria, tristeza, suspenso, misterio, aventura, combate, asombro. Jev returning `unknown` counts as low confidence and goes to the Muse override, which may return only the 8 ids. A hard failure stores no vector and the scene keeps the previous track. Never fake an emotion.
78|- Jev runs at `POST https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone` with the model pinned to `jev-1.14.0`.
79|- Public-domain books only.
80|- Images follow the book text and the W. W. Denslow 1900 illustrations: silver shoes, nothing from the 1939 MGM film.
81|- Never copy code from github.com/martinmw13/lectoria.
82|- Test with the cheapest models (Contributor). Use Standard for the final pass and the public chat.
83|
84|## Product rules
85|
86|Owner decisions. Short and binding.
87|
88|- Desktop first. No mobile or iOS work now.
89|- The reader shows one scene at a time. Sub-pages split long scenes by length only. Music cues run on scene entry.
90|- A chapter holds several scenes. Each scene has its own emotion.
91|- Paragraph ids carry a global ordinal `n`. Compare `n`, never id strings.
92|- `book.json` is frozen with a `textVersion` hash. Every cache key includes it.
93|- Scenes cover each chapter's paragraphs with no gaps and no overlaps. No scene crosses a chapter boundary. Scenes split at strong sequential emotion shifts; blends stay in the vector.
94|- Emotions are distributions. Each scene stores the full Jev probability vector over the 8 ids, plus `intensity` (0 to 1) and `tempo` (energy, 0 to 1). The Muse override on low confidence edits the vector and records that it did. It never swaps in a single label.
95|- Music is about 15 tracks, pre-generated offline with MusicGen on Modal as one coherent soundtrack: same orchestra and instrumentation, same leitmotif style. Each track is a weighted blend of emotions and carries an emotion vector plus intensity and tempo. The proposed way to pick the blends: cluster the Oz scene vectors and use the centroids as track prompts.
96|- The player picks the track nearest to the scene vector, by cosine similarity over the vector plus intensity and tempo. Hysteresis stops it from flipping on small changes. Skip or change track overrides until the next scene.
97|- The owner listens to short clips before any full generation. Agents do not run Modal until the owner says so.
98|- MusicGen weights are CC-BY-NC. The hackathon demo is non-commercial. The generated tracks must say so in their README.
99|- Chat is low priority and simple. The context is the book text up to the reader's current position. The book prefix goes first and the question goes last, so readers share the prompt cache. Oz is about 55k tokens.
100|- The chat system prompt answers only from the provided text. It refuses knowledge beyond it, even if the model knows the book.
101|- A spoiler mode toggle is for readers who finished the book. It sends the whole text so they can ask about later events. No live Glimmer spoiler guard. No per-chapter summaries for chat. Citing passages is optional.
102|- Glimmer (open weights) keeps a pipeline role. Current decision: it writes the per-scene "why this music" explanation shown in the Developer View.
103|- Spikes come before feature code. Throwaway scripts in `scripts/spikes/` measure Muse Image (response format, latency, Denslow-style prompt), Meta `json_schema` structured output, and the Jev vector on a few Oz scenes. Results go to `docs/spikes.md`.
104|- Spend is counted in integer micro-dollars. Reserve with Redis `INCRBY` before each model call and refund with `DECRBY` after. Reserve per call, including retries.
105|- The server clamps every model tool argument. Tool arguments are untrusted input.
106|- The CSP allows `challenges.cloudflare.com` (script and frame) and `*.public.blob.vercel-storage.com` (images).
107|- The "Picture this" cache key is the book plus the paragraph where the selection starts plus `textVersion` plus `promptVersion`. Never generate the same image twice for one paragraph. The prompt is built from that paragraph plus scene context.
108|- The "Picture scene" cache key is the book plus the scene id plus `textVersion` plus `promptVersion`.
109|- Images live in Vercel Blob at deterministic public paths (`addRandomSuffix: false`, `allowOverwrite: false`). An index in Upstash Redis maps key to Blob URL so hits are one Redis GET; on an index miss check the Blob path with `head()` before generating and backfill the index. Routes return Blob URLs, never image bytes.
110|- Modal endpoints require proxy auth. Tokens live only in env.
111|
112|## Security rules
113|
114|Summary. The full rules live in [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md).
115|
116|- Secrets live only in env vars: `.env.local` locally (gitignored), Vercel env vars in prod.
117|- `.env.example` holds names only, never values.
118|- Never use a `NEXT_PUBLIC_` variable for a secret. Only public ids such as the Turnstile site key may use it.
119|- `core/` stays pure: no keys, no env reads, no network clients, no `server-only`. Key-holding clients live in `server/` (Next.js only, each file starts with `import 'server-only'`) and in `pipeline/` (Node scripts that read env). Callers inject them into `core` functions as arguments. Tests run `core` with fake clients.
120|- The pre-commit secret scan must pass. Never bypass it with `--no-verify`.
121|- Errors to the client are generic. Details go to server logs only, never with keys.
122|- Never log request headers.
123|
124|## Writing rules
125|
126|Run docs, UI copy, and commit messages through the `unslop` skill: no filler, no hype, no emoji in headings, none of seamless, elevate, delve, robust, leverage. Headings use sentence case. Commit messages use an imperative subject under 72 chars, and the body says why.
127|
128|## Design
129|
130|Minimalist, functional, elegant. No generic AI-template look: no purple or violet anywhere, no gradient blobs, no glassmorphism, no emoji icons, no stock hero sections.
131|
132|The palette comes from Meta's brand. Meta blue `#0866FF` is the single accent, `#0064E0` for hover and pressed states. Text is near-black `#1C2B33`. Surfaces are white `#FFFFFF` and soft gray `#F1F4F7`. Dark mode keeps the same accent on a near-black surface: `#0B1215` surface, `#E4E6EB` text.
133|
134|The layout is typography-first. The book sits centered with a comfortable measure, about 60 to 70 chars per line. The companion chat lives in a quiet side panel. Whitespace is generous, the accent color is single, motion is subtle: under 200 ms, and it respects `prefers-reduced-motion`.
135|
136|These values live as CSS custom properties in [app/tokens.css](app/tokens.css), which is the source of truth.
137|
138|## Hooks
139|
140|`npm install` (or `npm run prepare`) points `core.hooksPath` at `.githooks`. The `pre-commit` hook rejects staged files over 5000 tokens and staged secrets. The `prepare-commit-msg` hook adds the co-author trailer. Run the checks by hand with `npm run check:size` and `npm run check:secrets`, and the hook tests with `npm run test:hooks`.

Read text file `SECURITY.md`.
1|# Security
2|
3|## Report a vulnerability
4|
5|Use GitHub private vulnerability reporting on this repo. Do not open a public issue for a security bug.
6|
7|## What is in place now
8|
9|- Secrets live only in env vars. `.env.example` holds names, never values.
10|- A pre-commit scan blocks staged secrets: gitleaks when installed, plus the built-in scanner in `scripts/check-secrets.mjs`, which always runs.
11|- Scans cover all tracked paths except lockfiles, including `agent-logs/`, `public/`, and `.agents/skills/`. CI runs the built-in scanner with `--all` plus pinned gitleaks v8.28.0 with a hardcoded sha256, and GitHub Actions pinned to commit SHAs.
12|- `.gitleaks.toml` extends the default gitleaks config and allowlists only the known test placeholder strings, never paths.
13|- GitHub secret scanning and push protection guard the remote.
14|- Dependabot alerts track vulnerable dependencies.
15|
16|## Rules for later tasks
17|
18|Planned, not built yet. Each app task implements its share.
19|
20|- The BYOK Meta key is never stored server-side or in logs. It stays in the browser session (`sessionStorage`) and travels over HTTPS per request in a header.
21|- The owner `META_API_KEY` funds the public chat and images within the per-person quota and the global cap. Once a person's quota is used, they may bring their own key (BYOK). A BYOK request uses only the user's key and never falls back to the owner key.
22|- BYOK requests are still rate-limited per IP.
23|- Logged error objects hold no keys, tokens, or raw provider output.
24|- HMAC comparisons run in constant time.
25|- The CSP allows `challenges.cloudflare.com` for scripts and frames, and `*.public.blob.vercel-storage.com` for images.
26|- Modal endpoints require proxy auth. Proxy tokens live only in env and travel as Modal-Key / Modal-Secret headers.
27|- Spend is counted in integer micro-dollars: reserve with Redis `INCRBY` before each model call, refund with `DECRBY` after.
28|- The anonymous session cookie is signed with HMAC (`SESSION_SECRET`) and set httpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Lax.
29|- IPs are stored only as salted hashes (`IP_HASH_SALT`) with daily keys.
30|- Quotas are strict per person: 15 questions and 5 images per day, counted by hashed IP and anonymous cookie, whichever runs out first. A global spend cap in Redis sits above them.
31|- Turnstile runs once per session.
32|- Errors never return stack traces or raw exception text.
33|- Book source files (epub, raw text) are never publicly served. Only processed public-domain JSON leaves the server.
34|- Security headers and a CSP live in `next.config.ts`.
35|- Input limits hold: question 500 chars, passage 600 chars. The server verifies each passage against the book text.

3|description: "Apply when you write, change, or keep a test. Assert what the code's users can observe, so that the test fails when that behavior breaks and keeps passing when only the internals change."

6|
7|# Test Behavior, Not Implementation
8|
9|A test is a claim about what the code does for its users: a caller, an end user, or another service. Behavior is what those users can observe through the interface they use. That includes return values, errors, state they can read back, and effects on systems outside the code, such as a request sent, a row written, or a message emitted. Implementation is what they cannot observe: private helpers, internal call order, intermediate data, and which internal collaborator did the work.
10|
11|Judge each test against two imagined edits:
12|
13|- **Break the behavior.** Make the code return a wrong value, skip an effect, or do the effect twice. If the test still passes, it proves nothing. The usual causes are an assertion looser than the contract, an expected value computed by the code under test, a restated constant or prompt string that never runs the code that reads it, and an assertion on data that the test built itself.
14|- **Change the internals.** Keep every observable result the same and restructure the code underneath. If the test now fails, it is pinned to the implementation. It will need a rewrite on every refactor and still catches no bug.
15|
16|Keep a test that catches the first edit and survives the second. Rewrite or delete the rest. To write a test that does both, drive the code through its users' interface with a concrete input. Derive the expected value from the requirement, not from a run of the code. Assert what the contract promises, no less and no more.
17|
18|The contract decides, not the shape of the assertion. When "an empty cart never charges" is the promise, an assertion that the payment client got no call is behavior. Pair it with a case where the charge happens, so that the test shows it can see a call. The payload that a mocked external service receives is behavior, because that service observes it. A call to an internal helper is implementation, because no user can see it. An empty list is the exact answer when no record matches, and a hollow check when the test only needs some result. An exact error message pins wording that no caller reads. The error type that callers branch on is the contract.
19|
20|A test can pin an invariant instead of a call, such as a key that must exist in two tables or a compile-time type check. The invariant is the behavior.

17|| Simplest total type | Keep `T[]` while every operation on it stays total. Strengthen to `NonEmpty<T>` only where the loose type forces `!`, a cast, or a "should never happen" throw. |
18|| `unknown` over `any` | External data is `unknown`. |
19|| Schemas before guards | Before hand-writing a property-by-property type guard, use the repository's runtime schema library and infer the type from the schema, such as `z.infer`. |
20|| No `as` casts | Every `as` is a runtime crash waiting. Cast only after validation. |

3|description: "Apply when you write, change, or keep a test. Assert what the code's users can observe, so that the test fails when that behavior breaks and keeps passing when only the internals change."
4|disable-model-invocation: true
5|---
6|
7|# Test Behavior, Not Implementation
8|
9|A test is a claim about what the code does for its users: a caller, an end user, or another service. Behavior is what those users can observe through the interface they use. That includes return values, errors, state they can read back, and effects on systems outside the code, such as a request sent, a row written, or a message emitted. Implementation is what they cannot observe: private helpers, internal call order, intermediate data, and which internal collaborator did the work.
10|
11|Judge each test against two imagined edits:
12|
13|- **Break the behavior.** Make the code return a wrong value, skip an effect, or do the effect twice. If the test still passes, it proves nothing. The usual causes are an assertion looser than the contract, an expected value computed by the code under test, a restated constant or prompt string that never runs the code that reads it, and an assertion on data that the test built itself.
14|- **Change the internals.** Keep every observable result the same and restructure the code underneath. If the test now fails, it is pinned to the implementation. It will need a rewrite on every refactor and still catches no bug.
15|
16|Keep a test that catches the first edit and survives the second. Rewrite or delete the rest. To write a test that does both, drive the code through its users' interface with a concrete input. Derive the expected value from the requirement, not from a run of the code. Assert what the contract promises, no less and no more.
17|
18|The contract decides, not the shape of the assertion. When "an empty cart never charges" is the promise, an assertion that the payment client got no call is behavior. Pair it with a case where the charge happens, so that the test shows it can see a call. The payload that a mocked external service receives is behavior, because that service observes it. A call to an internal helper is implementation, because no user can see it. An empty list is the exact answer when no record matches, and a hollow check when the test only needs some result. An exact error message pins wording that no caller reads. The error type that callers branch on is the contract.
19|
20|A test can pin an invariant instead of a call, such as a key that must exist in two tables or a compile-time type check. The invariant is the behavior.

18|and tempo. It never sees `jev`, `muse_override`, or provenance.

110|## Selection

113|There is one mode only. Every scheduled select ranges over all tracks in
114|the current style and draws among the tracks with the scene emotion (or
115|the best same-style tracks when the emotion is missing) within

118|the user's choice, changed with the style selector. The default style is

130|## Next track and style change
131|
132|`nextTrack` cycles same-emotion tracks in score order across the whole
133|style, wrapping and skipping the current, then the best same-style track
134|overall when the emotion is missing. A null scene cycles the style set
135|in id order. One track or none gives null.
136|
137|`requestStyleChange` picks the best match for the scene in the new style
138|by score. It never crosses styles. The scheduler applies it at once
139|with the normal crossfade and holds the choice like a Next. There is no
140|mix toggle and no soundtrack-change button.

142|## Playlist mode
143|

145|plays. `enterPlaylist` switches at once to the first `trackIds` entry
146|with `crossfadeSec`, no dwell and no min-track rule. While it is on,
147|scene changes update the active scene but never switch, `requestNext`

149|the last to the first, and playlist tracks run to their end because the

154|the style list hides styles with only playlist tracks.

156|## Similarity and config
157|
158|`Similarity = (scene, track, weights) => number`, where
159|`SceneSignal = { vector, intensity, tempo }`. The default is
160|`bhattacharyyaSimilarity`: both 8-emotion vectors renormalize to sum 1

165|a weights override changes the ranking. `cosineSimilarity` over
166|`buildFeatures` output stays as an exported alternative. One exported object,
167|`MUSIC_CONFIG`, holds `similarity`, `weights`, `dwellSec` (20),
168|`sceneEntryDwellSec` (5), `minTrackSec` (45), `crossfadeSec` (3), and
169|`randomTolerance` (0.05). Everything else reads from it. Ranking ties go
170|to the lower track id. Route entries use `sceneEntryDwellSec` as the
171|dwell override; scoring and overrides are unchanged. One path scopes,
172|ranks, and draws: `audibleTracks` is the one playlist-only filter,
173|`compareTrackId` the one tie-break, `rankScored` scores each track once
174|(best first, ties to lower id), and `selectScheduled` runs the tolerance
175|window, keep-current, and min-track hold with one rng call per draw.
176|
177|## Music session
178|

180|The reader sends intents (`sceneEntered`, `tick`, `skip`, `previous`,
181|`styleChanged`, `trackEnded`, `playlistToggled`) through
182|`startSession` and `dispatch` with explicit `nowSec` and `rng` values,
183|so all timing is testable without timers or a render. `dispatch`
184|returns the same session object when nothing changed, so the 1 s tick
185|rerenders nothing. The reader cues music on scene entry only: one
186|`sceneEntered` per route id, gated by an id comparison, so sub-page
187|moves never reach the session. The session holds the scheduler state,
188|the Previous history, the selection, the fade, and the replay nonce,
189|and derives the view the player renders: track id, fade, nonce,
190|canPrev/canSkip, playlist flag, style.
191|
192|## Selection scheduler
193|
194|`core/music-schedule.ts` is a pure state machine. The session calls
195|`observeScene`, `tickScheduler`, `requestNext`, `noteTrackEnded`,
196|`requestManualTrack`, `switchStyle`, `enterPlaylist`, and
197|`exitPlaylist` with explicit `nowSec` values, so all timing is testable
198|without timers. State holds the current track id and when it started, the active
199|scene id, the pending scene id and since when, and the skip override
200|with the scene it belongs to.
201|
202|A newly entered scene becomes pending and the dwell clock restarts, so
203|fast scrolling keeps only the newest scene. The first track ever plays
204|at once with no dwell. After the pending scene holds for `dwellSec` it
205|becomes active and the override clears. Then a scheduled select draws
206|among the in-style tracks within `randomTolerance` of the best score,
207|keeping the current track when it is eligible, and switches to the
208|drawn track only once the current track played `minTrackSec`. A tick
209|passes the active scene back through the same draw, so a hold from
210|`minTrackSec` releases on time, unless a skip override stands: ticks
211|return no change while it is set, and only a new scene promotion
212|clears it. A switch reports the normal crossfade length (3 s, 0 s for
213|the first track ever). The skip choice holds until the next scene change;
214|after that, dwell and the draw apply with the override track as the
215|current track. A null scene means a failed analysis with no vector, so
216|it never triggers a switch. A non-looping track that ends fades into
217|the best remaining track, excluding the one that ended, and clears the
218|skip override.
219|
220|## Player
221|
222|`app/player.tsx` takes the track, `replayNonce`, the fade length for
223|the latest switch, `canPrev`/`canSkip` with their handlers, volume and
224|mute with their handlers, the style list with the current style and its
225|handler, the end-of-track handler, and the playlist props
226|(`playlistOn`, `playlistLabel`, `onTogglePlaylist`,
227|`controlsDisabled`). It owns two `audio`
228|elements, play state, volume, and the equal-power crossfade
229|(cos/sin gains over the fade time, driven by `requestAnimationFrame`).
230|It never uses the `loop` attribute. Volume lives in a ref, so the slider
231|never re-runs the track effect or touches `src`. A new track request
232|mid-fade cancels the pending fade and fades from the audible element to
233|the newest track. On load each track seeks to `startSec` once metadata
234|is available. Long tracks with `loop` true crossfade into the other
235|element playing the same track from `startSec` when `currentTime`
236|reaches `duration - fade`, where `fade` is the latest scheduler fade
237|length, or the config `crossfadeSec` when none was reported yet. When
238|`loop` is false the player reports the end and the scheduler picks the
239|next-best track excluding the ended one. Pause stops both elements and
240|freezes the fade in place; play resumes the audible elements from the
241|frozen point. Audio starts once, on the first press, with fade 0.
242|Audio starts only after the user presses play. Reduced motion is read in
243|state with a change listener and affects visuals only, never the fade.
244|
245|The bar is one sticky row, 56 px tall: the `Lectoria` wordmark left,
246|the player centre, the Chopin button and the source icon link right.
247|The inner row is centered with 24 px side padding, one bottom hairline
248|in the border token, and nothing touching the viewport edges. The inner
249|max-width is 56rem, wider than the 65ch book column on purpose so the
250|full now-playing line fits at 1280 px. The player holds Previous,
251|Play/Pause, Next, the now-playing line (flexible space, `min-width`
252|16rem, truncated with an ellipsis, full line in the `title` tooltip),
253|a mute icon button (`aria-pressed`, `aria-label` `Mute` / `Unmute`, the
254|icon shows the muted state), a volume slider with `aria-label` `Volume`
255|(96 px) next to it, a style selector with `aria-label`
256|`Orchestra / Piano` and no visible label text listing only styles that
257|have tracks (hidden while fewer than two qualify), then the Chopin
258|button and the source icon link. The transport and mute buttons and the
259|source icon link are icon-only inline SVGs (`currentColor`, 32 px hit
260|area), quiet and neutral, Meta blue on hover and focus-visible, each
261|with `aria-label` and `title`; the source link reads `Music source
262|(opens in new tab)`. Previous walks the session history and restarts
263|the current track with no history, including the current playlist piece
264|in playlist mode; Next cycles same-emotion tracks in the style.
265|A `Just play Chopin` round image button (`/art/chopin-just-play-me.png`,
266|40 px, `alt` and `aria-label` `Just play Chopin`) appears only when
267|the manifest defines that playlist with tracks; it carries
268|`aria-pressed`, and while pressed it shows a 2 px Meta-blue ring plus
269|scale 1.05. The now-playing line shows `display title · composer
270|· source`: `displayTitle` drops quoted nicknames, key phrases, and
271|opus/catalogue suffixes from the track title, and the source is the
272|artist plus ` / <platform>` when the attribution names Musopen or
273|Jamendo and the artist does not already say it, dropped when it would
274|repeat the performer. The full manifest title plus the license and full
275|attribution sits in the `title` tooltip. On manifest failure the reader
276|still renders and the bar shows a short neutral note. UI motion stays
277|under 200 ms. Controls are real buttons and inputs with labels, visible
278|focus, and keyboard use. `app/player.tsx` keeps the audio engine,
279|transport, and bar layout; `app/player-controls.tsx` holds the style
280|selector and the playlist toggle; `app/music-prefs.ts` owns the storage
281|helper. The heading keeps `h2:focus:not(:focus-visible){outline:none}`
282|so mouse navigation shows no box while keyboard focus keeps its ring.
283|No user-visible emotion labels exist; ids stay as they are.
284|`core/music-credit.ts` builds the line as a pure function with tests,
285|including the pure `displayTitle`.
286|`core/music-history.ts` is the bounded history stack the session banks
287|automatic switches on; `requestManualTrack` in `core/music-schedule.ts`
288|holds a manual pick.
289|
290|## Image api
291|
292|`POST /api/images` (Node runtime, `maxDuration` 120). Request is a
293|discriminated union: `{ kind: "passage", bookId, textVersion, n }` names
294|the paragraph where the selection starts, `{ kind: "scene", bookId,
295|textVersion, sceneId }` names the scene. Validation is strict: known
296|book, matching `textVersion`, integer `n` inside the book, known
297|`sceneId`. Any other body is a 400 with a generic English message.
298|The client sends ordinals and ids only, never text. "Illustrate
299|scene" uses the scene id from the route.
300|
301|Responses (typed in `core/types.ts`): `{ status: "ready", url, cached,
302|caption }` with a Vercel Blob URL, never bytes; `{ status: "pending" }`
303|when another request holds the lock, in which case the client reposts
304|every 3 s up to about 2 minutes; `{ status: "error", code, message }`
305|where code is `quota`, `budget`, `unavailable`, or `bad_request` with a
306|friendly English message. Caption is the scene title for scenes and the
307|first words of the paragraph for passages, built server-side.
308|
309|The passage cache key is book plus start paragraph plus `textVersion`
310|plus `PROMPT_VERSION` (`v1`); the scene key is book plus scene id plus
311|the same versions. Both map to a deterministic Blob path
312|(`addRandomSuffix: false`, `allowOverwrite: false`). An Upstash Redis
313|index maps key to Blob URL, so hits are one GET; on an index miss the
314|server lists by exact path prefix (head equivalent) before generating
315|and backfills the index.
316|A Redis lock per key returns `pending` to concurrent requests. Quota is
317|5 new images per person per day by hashed IP and signed cookie,
318|whichever runs out first; a shared spend counter in integer
319|micro-dollars sits under `SPEND_CAP_USD` (default 10). Failures refund
320|quota and budget and release the lock.
321|
322|## Chat api
323|
324|Contract only, no routes. Request `{ bookId, textVersion, positionN,
325|spoilerMode, messages }` carries the chat history and the reader
326|position. The response is streamed text. The server builds context from
327|the book text up to `positionN`, or the whole book when `spoilerMode` is
328|on, with the book prefix first and the question last so readers share
329|the prompt cache. The system prompt answers only from that text and
330|refuses the rest. Types live in `core/types.ts`.
331|
332|## Quotas and budget
333|
334|Server only. Spend is counted in integer micro-dollars: reserve with
335|Redis `INCRBY` before each model call, refund with `DECRBY` after, one
336|reserve per call including retries. The server clamps every model tool
337|argument. Clients never see keys or raw errors. Generic messages go to
338|the client, details stay in server logs.

68|optional `credit`. `Track = { id, src, title, emotion, vector,
69|intensity, tempo, durationSec, soundtrack, style }` plus optional
70|`startSec` (default 0, where playback starts on first play and on each
71|loop), `endSec` (default the media end, where the track stops or loops),
72|`gainDb` (default 0, a loudness trim in dB, in -24..12),
73|`loop` (default true), `source` (`generated`, `jamendo`, or
74|`recording`), `artist`, `composer`, `license`, `attribution`, and
75|`sourceUrl` (https only). `durationSec` is the playable length: the
76|segment end (or the file end) minus `startSec`. `startSec` and `endSec`
77|are absolute media times with `startSec < endSec`; `endSec` stays within
78|`startSec + durationSec`. The player scales volume by the track gain and
79|ends or loops at `effectiveEnd`, the earlier of `endSec` and the loaded
80|media end. `emotion` is the hand label: one of the 8
81|emotion ids in `core/types.ts`. The vector covers the 8 ids with finite
82|entries in 0..1. Every track names a soundtrack id, every track style
83|matches its soundtrack style, and every style is a listed style id.
84|`core/music.ts` owns `parseManifest`, which rejects unknown versions,
85|duplicate ids, unknown soundtrack or style ids, style mismatches,
86|missing fields, bad vectors, NaN entries, out-of-range numbers,
87|a negative `startSec`, a bad `gainDb` or `endSec`, unknown `source`
88|values, a non-boolean
89|`playlistOnly`, and any `src`
90|that is not a `/music/` path or `https` URL. Unknown fields stay
91|ignored. A soundtrack with no
92|tracks parses. The reader calls it on every fetch, so a bad drop-in
93|fails loudly in dev. Remote audio lives on one Blob store, so
94|`media-src` in `next.config.ts` lists exactly
95|`https://3vuhzq2wmortnuxj.public.blob.vercel-storage.com`. Build the
96|manifest with `npm run build:music data/music/labels.json
97|data/music/library.json --out public/music/manifest.json`, which runs
98|`pipeline/labels-to-manifest.ts` and validates the result before
99|writing.
100|
101|`Track.playlistOnly` defaults to false. A true value marks a playlist
102|only track: it still names a soundtrack and style, but no emotion pick
103|ever returns it. `MusicManifest.playlists` holds
104|`Playlist = { id, label, trackIds }` entries, most notably
105|`just-play-chopin`. A missing key parses as an empty list, and a v2
106|migration gives an empty list. Parse rejects duplicate playlist ids,
107|empty labels, non-array `trackIds`, and any `trackIds` entry that names
108|no track, with the playlist and the id in the message.
109|
110|## Selection
111|
112|`MusicSelection = { style }` is the session: `style` scopes every pick.
113|There is one mode only. Every scheduled select ranges over all tracks in
114|the current style and draws among the tracks with the scene emotion (or
115|the best same-style tracks when the emotion is missing) within
116|`randomTolerance` (0.05) of the best score, keeps the current track when
117|it is eligible, and avoids an immediate repeat otherwise. The style is
118|the user's choice, changed with the style selector. The default style is
119|the first listed style with tracks; a stored style with tracks wins. The
120|session persists `{ style, volume, muted }` in localStorage under
121|`lectoria.music.v1`. Old values with `mode` or `soundtrackId` load by
122|`style` alone and ignore unknown fields; a stored object without
123|`volume` or `muted` loads `volume: null` and `muted: false`. A bad
124|`volume` (not a finite number in 0..1) loads null and the player starts
125|at 0.8; a bad `muted` loads false. A stored style with no tracks falls
126|back to the default. Storage exceptions never break playback. Dwell
127|and min-track rules hold. The core never calls `Math.random`; the
128|reader injects it and tests pass a seeded stub.
129|
130|## Next track and style change
131|
132|`nextTrack` cycles same-emotion tracks in score order across the whole
133|style, wrapping and skipping the current, then the best same-style track
134|overall when the emotion is missing. A null scene cycles the style set
135|in id order. One track or none gives null.
136|
137|`requestStyleChange` picks the best match for the scene in the new style
138|by score. It never crosses styles. The scheduler applies it at once
139|with the normal crossfade and holds the choice like a Next. There is no
140|mix toggle and no soundtrack-change button.
141|
142|## Playlist mode
143|
144|`SchedulerState.playlist` holds `{ id, index }` while a fixed playlist
145|plays. `enterPlaylist` switches at once to the first `trackIds` entry
146|with `crossfadeSec`, no dwell and no min-track rule. While it is on,
147|scene changes update the active scene but never switch, `requestNext`
148|and `noteTrackEnded` advance to the next entry in order and wrap from
149|the last to the first, and playlist tracks run to their end because the
150|player forces looping off. `exitPlaylist` clears the playlist state and
151|switches at once to the best match for the current scene under the
152|restored selection. The playlist is never persisted, so a reload returns
153|to emotion mode. The style selector stays disabled while it is on, and
154|the style list hides styles with only playlist tracks.
155|
156|## Similarity and config
157|
158|`Similarity = (scene, track, weights) => number`, where
159|`SceneSignal = { vector, intensity, tempo }`. The default is
160|`bhattacharyyaSimilarity`: both 8-emotion vectors renormalize to sum 1
161|(an all-zero vector gives an affinity of 0), `E` is the sum of
162|`sqrt(s_k * t_k)`, and the score is `weights.emotion * E` plus
163|`weights.intensity` and `weights.tempo` each for intensity and tempo
164|closeness. Scoring and ranking pass the resolved config weights in, so
165|a weights override changes the ranking. `cosineSimilarity` over
166|`buildFeatures` output stays as an exported alternative. One exported object,
167|`MUSIC_CONFIG`, holds `similarity`, `weights`, `dwellSec` (20),
168|`sceneEntryDwellSec` (5), `minTrackSec` (45), `crossfadeSec` (3), and
169|`randomTolerance` (0.05). Everything else reads from it. Ranking ties go
170|to the lower track id. Route entries use `sceneEntryDwellSec` as the
171|dwell override; scoring and overrides are unchanged. One path scopes,
172|ranks, and draws: `audibleTracks` is the one playlist-only filter,
173|`compareTrackId` the one tie-break, `rankScored` scores each track once
174|(best first, ties to lower id), and `selectScheduled` runs the tolerance
175|window, keep-current, and min-track hold with one rng call per draw.
176|
177|## Music session
178|
179|`core/music-session.ts` is the single policy owner behind the reader.
180|The reader sends intents (`sceneEntered`, `tick`, `skip`, `previous`,
181|`styleChanged`, `trackEnded`, `playlistToggled`) through
182|`startSession` and `dispatch` with explicit `nowSec` and `rng` values,
183|so all timing is testable without timers or a render. `dispatch`
184|returns the same session object when nothing changed, so the 1 s tick
185|rerenders nothing. The reader cues music on scene entry only: one
186|`sceneEntered` per route id, gated by an id comparison, so sub-page
187|moves never reach the session. The session holds the scheduler state,
188|the Previous history, the selection, the fade, and the replay nonce,
189|and derives the view the player renders: track id, fade, nonce,
190|canPrev/canSkip, playlist flag, style.
191|
192|## Selection scheduler
193|
194|`core/music-schedule.ts` is a pure state machine. The session calls
195|`observeScene`, `tickScheduler`, `requestNext`, `noteTrackEnded`,
196|`requestManualTrack`, `switchStyle`, `enterPlaylist`, and
197|`exitPlaylist` with explicit `nowSec` values, so all timing is testable
198|without timers. State holds the current track id and when it started, the active
199|scene id, the pending scene id and since when, and the skip override
200|with the scene it belongs to.
201|
202|A newly entered scene becomes pending and the dwell clock restarts, so
203|fast scrolling keeps only the newest scene. The first track ever plays
204|at once with no dwell. After the pending scene holds for `dwellSec` it
205|becomes active and the override clears. Then a scheduled select draws
206|among the in-style tracks within `randomTolerance` of the best score,
207|keeping the current track when it is eligible, and switches to the
208|drawn track only once the current track played `minTrackSec`. A tick
209|passes the active scene back through the same draw, so a hold from
210|`minTrackSec` releases on time, unless a skip override stands: ticks
211|return no change while it is set, and only a new scene promotion
212|clears it. A switch reports the normal crossfade length (3 s, 0 s for
213|the first track ever). The skip choice holds until the next scene change;
214|after that, dwell and the draw apply with the override track as the
215|current track. A null scene means a failed analysis with no vector, so
216|it never triggers a switch. A non-looping track that ends fades into
217|the best remaining track, excluding the one that ended, and clears the
218|skip override.
219|
220|## Player
221|
222|`app/player.tsx` takes the track, `replayNonce`, the fade length for
223|the latest switch, `canPrev`/`canSkip` with their handlers, volume and
224|mute with their handlers, the style list with the current style and its
225|handler, the end-of-track handler, and the playlist props
226|(`playlistOn`, `playlistLabel`, `onTogglePlaylist`,
227|`controlsDisabled`). It owns two `audio`
228|elements, play state, volume, and the equal-power crossfade
229|(cos/sin gains over the fade time, driven by `requestAnimationFrame`).
230|It never uses the `loop` attribute. Volume lives in a ref, so the slider
231|never re-runs the track effect or touches `src`. A new track request
232|mid-fade cancels the pending fade and fades from the audible element to
233|the newest track. On load each track seeks to `startSec` once metadata
234|is available. Long tracks with `loop` true crossfade into the other
235|element playing the same track from `startSec` when `currentTime`
236|reaches `duration - fade`, where `fade` is the latest scheduler fade
237|length, or the config `crossfadeSec` when none was reported yet. When
238|`loop` is false the player reports the end and the scheduler picks the
239|next-best track excluding the ended one. Pause stops both elements and
240|freezes the fade in place; play resumes the audible elements from the
241|frozen point. Audio starts once, on the first press, with fade 0.
242|Audio starts only after the user presses play. Reduced motion is read in
243|state with a change listener and affects visuals only, never the fade.
244|
245|The bar is one sticky row, 56 px tall: the `Lectoria` wordmark left,
246|the player centre, the Chopin button and the source icon link right.
247|The inner row is centered with 24 px side padding, one bottom hairline
248|in the border token, and nothing touching the viewport edges. The inner
249|max-width is 56rem, wider than the 65ch book column on purpose so the
250|full now-playing line fits at 1280 px. The player holds Previous,
251|Play/Pause, Next, the now-playing line (flexible space, `min-width`
252|16rem, truncated with an ellipsis, full line in the `title` tooltip),
253|a mute icon button (`aria-pressed`, `aria-label` `Mute` / `Unmute`, the
254|icon shows the muted state), a volume slider with `aria-label` `Volume`
255|(96 px) next to it, a style selector with `aria-label`
256|`Orchestra / Piano` and no visible label text listing only styles that
257|have tracks (hidden while fewer than two qualify), then the Chopin
258|button and the source icon link. The transport and mute buttons and the
259|source icon link are icon-only inline SVGs (`currentColor`, 32 px hit
260|area), quiet and neutral, Meta blue on hover and focus-visible, each
261|with `aria-label` and `title`; the source link reads `Music source
262|(opens in new tab)`. Previous walks the session history and restarts
263|the current track with no history, including the current playlist piece
264|in playlist mode; Next cycles same-emotion tracks in the style.
265|A `Just play Chopin` round image button (`/art/chopin-just-play-me.png`,
266|40 px, `alt` and `aria-label` `Just play Chopin`) appears only when
267|the manifest defines that playlist with tracks; it carries
268|`aria-pressed`, and while pressed it shows a 2 px Meta-blue ring plus
269|scale 1.05. The now-playing line shows `display title · composer
270|· source`: `displayTitle` drops quoted nicknames, key phrases, and
271|opus/catalogue suffixes from the track title, and the source is the
272|artist plus ` / <platform>` when the attribution names Musopen or
273|Jamendo and the artist does not already say it, dropped when it would
274|repeat the performer. The full manifest title plus the license and full
275|attribution sits in the `title` tooltip. On manifest failure the reader
276|still renders and the bar shows a short neutral note. UI motion stays
277|under 200 ms. Controls are real buttons and inputs with labels, visible
278|focus, and keyboard use. `app/player.tsx` keeps the audio engine,
279|transport, and bar layout; `app/player-controls.tsx` holds the style
280|selector and the playlist toggle; `app/music-prefs.ts` owns the storage
281|helper. The heading keeps `h2:focus:not(:focus-visible){outline:none}`
282|so mouse navigation shows no box while keyboard focus keeps its ring.
283|No user-visible emotion labels exist; ids stay as they are.
284|`core/music-credit.ts` builds the line as a pure function with tests,
285|including the pure `displayTitle`.
286|`core/music-history.ts` is the bounded history stack the session banks
287|automatic switches on; `requestManualTrack` in `core/music-schedule.ts`
288|holds a manual pick.
289|
290|## Image api
291|
292|`POST /api/images` (Node runtime, `maxDuration` 120). Request is a
293|discriminated union: `{ kind: "passage", bookId, textVersion, n }` names
294|the paragraph where the selection starts, `{ kind: "scene", bookId,
295|textVersion, sceneId }` names the scene. Validation is strict: known
296|book, matching `textVersion`, integer `n` inside the book, known
297|`sceneId`. Any other body is a 400 with a generic English message.
298|The client sends ordinals and ids only, never text. "Illustrate
299|scene" uses the scene id from the route.
300|
301|Responses (typed in `core/types.ts`): `{ status: "ready", url, cached,
302|caption }` with a Vercel Blob URL, never bytes; `{ status: "pending" }`
303|when another request holds the lock, in which case the client reposts
304|every 3 s up to about 2 minutes; `{ status: "error", code, message }`
305|where code is `quota`, `budget`, `unavailable`, or `bad_request` with a
306|friendly English message. Caption is the scene title for scenes and the
307|first words of the paragraph for passages, built server-side.
308|
309|The passage cache key is book plus start paragraph plus `textVersion`
310|plus `PROMPT_VERSION` (`v1`); the scene key is book plus scene id plus
311|the same versions. Both map to a deterministic Blob path
312|(`addRandomSuffix: false`, `allowOverwrite: false`). An Upstash Redis
313|index maps key to Blob URL, so hits are one GET; on an index miss the
314|server lists by exact path prefix (head equivalent) before generating
315|and backfills the index.
316|A Redis lock per key returns `pending` to concurrent requests. Quota is
317|5 new images per person per day by hashed IP and signed cookie,
318|whichever runs out first; a shared spend counter in integer
319|micro-dollars sits under `SPEND_CAP_USD` (default 10). Failures refund
320|quota and budget and release the lock.
321|
322|## Chat api
323|
324|Contract only, no routes. Request `{ bookId, textVersion, positionN,
325|spoilerMode, messages }` carries the chat history and the reader
326|position. The response is streamed text. The server builds context from
327|the book text up to `positionN`, or the whole book when `spoilerMode` is
328|on, with the book prefix first and the question last so readers share
329|the prompt cache. The system prompt answers only from that text and
330|refuses the rest. Types live in `core/types.ts`.
331|
332|## Quotas and budget
333|
334|Server only. Spend is counted in integer micro-dollars: reserve with
335|Redis `INCRBY` before each model call, refund with `DECRBY` after, one
336|reserve per call including retries. The server clamps every model tool
337|argument. Clients never see keys or raw errors. Generic messages go to
338|the client, details stay in server logs.

# Git source-control safety

The working tree belongs to the user. Make the change, leave it visible, and
let them decide what becomes history.

## Never without an explicit ask

The user must have asked for that exact write in this session, in their own
words. An explicit request to create a new commit counts anywhere in the user's
own task text, but it is not a request to amend, push, or tag. Finishing a task
without that request does not authorize a history write.

- `commit`, `commit --amend`, `push`, `tag`, `rebase`, `cherry-pick`, `revert`,
  `merge`, branch deletion, `reset --hard`, path restore, and `clean -f` all
  require an explicit ask.
- Never publish merely because publication would be useful.

## Before an authorized discard

Recovery is insurance, not authorization. A save never expands what the user
allowed you to delete or overwrite.

When the user explicitly authorized an operation that may discard or broadly
overwrite workspace changes, and the workspace is an ordinary Git checkout:

1. After `muse.read_skill` gives the physical Git skill package path, run:

   ```bash
   bash <git-skill-dir>/scripts/workspace-recovery.sh save before-discard
   ```

2. Keep the printed `refs/tbh/recovery/...` value in your handoff, then perform
   only the exact authorized operation.
3. If the save fails or the workspace is unsupported, stop before destruction
   and ask the user.

To recover that saved tree later, run:

```bash
bash <git-skill-dir>/scripts/workspace-recovery.sh restore <recovery-ref>
```

index in place, and restores the selected snapshot into the worktree. The ref
also retains distinct staged bytes when the same path had later worktree edits.
Read those staged bytes with `git show '<recovery-ref>^2:<path>'`; the recovery
commit's second parent is the saved index tree. Ignored files are not saved;
restore refuses an ignored-path collision rather than overwrite data it could
not save. Use only the exact printed ref, not a revision expression.

tool that requires a clean tree, are also fine when the original state is put
back afterward.

## The rest

- Do not use a broad add in a tree you did not clean; name the files you changed.
- Do not initialize a repository inside vendored, build, data, or existing
  source-control trees.

  `git status` look clean. "Leave the working tree clean", "tidy up", and

  stashing, or deleting the user's files; clean up only scratch you created
  and say the user's files remain.
- Do not hand-edit generated files; change their source of truth.
- Scratch repositories under a temporary directory are yours to experiment in.

## Locks and corrupt state

A Git lock usually means another process is writing. Never kill the holder on
your own initiative. Wait, inspect the holder read-only, use that tool's normal
stop mechanism, or report the block. Never delete a lock without proving no
live process owns it, and never respond to index corruption by deleting state
and committing anyway.

Never commit or push while status reports changes you did not make and cannot
explain.

## If you already made an unwanted write

Say so plainly and stop. Do not attempt more history surgery without direction.
